newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - MAY 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - MAY 6.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
- SWEDES BUY US MEDICAL COMPANY FOR 1.6 BILLION DOLLARS

Investment vehicle of Sweden's Wallenberg family, Incentive, have announced a 1.6 billion dollar takeover of America's second largest provider of dialysis services, Vivra. Incentive plans to merge Vivra with Gambro Group, the medical business that it bought last year. The bid is being made in part with the proceeds of the shares in the Electrolux appliances group which Incentive sold last year.
- LIFFE HAS BUSIEST APRIL ON RECORD

The London futures market, Liffe, announced that it traded a record 16 million futures and options contracts last month, representing an average daily nominal turnover of 151 billion stg. This was the busiest April ever for the market, with business 45 per cent higher on April of last year. Daniel Hodson, chief executive, claimed this was a result of speculation over factors such as Italian entry into EMU, a rise in US interest rates and the UK general election.
- MARKETS HIT HIGHS ON MOSTLY QUIET DAY

European markets were all on an upbeat mood yesterday with Germany, Switzerland and Belgium all reaching record highs, following the strength of Wall Street on Friday. However, Wall Street lost its early gain even though it was 35 points up at one point on hopes that the Federal Reserve will not increase short- term interest rates in the near future. Trading volume for yesterday was low due to holidays in London and Tokyo.
THE TIMES
- TUC MOBILISES PENSION POWER TO INFLUENCE SHELL BOARD

The TUC may introduce an initiative which could herald a new era in shareholder activism. The TUC is urging members who have influence over pension funds to cast their votes in the debate over the environmental and human rights policies of the multinational oil company Shell. Employees will have a powerful voice on issues of corporate responsibility, which was previously left to the discretion of fund managers.
- BUSANG CALLED WORLD'S WORST MINING FRAUD

According to the Canadian consultant Strathcona Mineral Services, the Indonesian gold discovery announced by Canada's Bre-X Minerals was based on data falsified on an "unprecedented" scale. It found no evidence of viable gold deposits in Busang's southeast zone, contrary to claims from Bre-X, and it would be unlikely that gold would ever be found in that sector.
- FIRMS FACE 'FLOOD' OF EU LABOUR LEGISLATION

Conservative economic spokesman in the European Parliament, Graham Mather, has claimed that a flood of costly and intrusive new workplace laws is likely to be poured into the European social chapter once Britain has joined the other 14 signatories. He said that medium-sized businesses would be worst hit. Some supporters of the social chapter claim that British firms face complex EU sexual harassment regulation and a directive to give part-time workers fully equal contract rights.
THE GUARDIAN
- TECHNOLOGY TYCOON IS TO TAKE HELM OF TORIES' PFI FLAGSHIP

The new paymaster-general and tycoon Geofrey Robinson is to take on the job of motivating economic growth as well as overseeing the Private Finance Initiative and privatisation portfolios. He appears to be an ideal candidate because he has his feet firmly placed in both business and Labour Party circles. He may appeal to company bosses who have been wary of the PFI as he has said that nothing should lose money.
- BOARD MEMBERS GET OUTSIDE PERKS

According to new research from Company Reporting, non- executive directors are involved in many deals, including consultancy contracts and preferential housing loans, with companies where they are supposed to be acting as independents in the boardroom. The study suggests it may be routine to find non- executives financially dependent on companies.
- SHAREHOLDERS SHAME SHELL

Oil company Shell is facing demands to improve on environmental and human rights issues, as two leading environmental and human rights organisations, Amnesty UK and World-Wide Fund for Nature, back a shareholders' resolution demanding higher standards. This will be the first time a big British company has faced a shareholders' resolution on environmental and human rights issues.
THE INDEPENDENT
- NEW DTI CHIEF TO SHAKE UP UTILITIES

The newly appointed DTI minister John Battle has said a high priority for Labour's trade and industry team would be a shake up of privatised utility regulation, putting greater emphasis on consumer interest. Battle has been given a wider-than-expected portfolio which is likely to include science and technology. President of the Board of Trade, Margaret Beckett, is planning to increase the powers of the DTI, giving it more responsibility for employment issues. - BUSINESS SPLIT OVER LABOUR ECONOMY

According to a poll of 600 businessmen across the country, carried out by Dun & Bradstreet, the business community is split on the new Government's ability to handle the economy. However, those who felt the impact of a new government would be positive outnumbered the negatives by six to four. Also, 40 per cent thought that the election result was not important for their business.
- ELECTRICAL MAKERS BLAMED FOR HIGH COSTS

According to a report by retail consultancy Verdict, customers are being overcharged for electrical goods because multinational manufacturers want to maintain profits and add cachet to their brands. Verdict exonerate from blame large retail chains such as Dixons and those run by the regional electricity companies, but it says consumers are being denied choice by the dominance of manufactures, thus preventing growth of a discount retail sector to match that in the US.
